title: Interfaces, Abstract Classes, and Dependency Injection
summary: Check classes against interfaces with implements, share code through abstract classes, and pass dependencies in through constructors so fakes can stand in.
intro: Real codebases are full of classes that play a role: a notifier, a repository, a clock, a pricing rule. This lesson covers the three tools TypeScript code uses for roles. `implements` checks that a class fits an interface. An abstract class shares code and leaves gaps that each subclass must fill. And dependency injection hands each role to the class that needs it, through its constructor, so a test or an example can pass in a fake. Every workspace codebase later in this course is wired this way.

steps.title: Implementing an interface

examples.title: Notifiers
examples.prompt: Write an email notifier and an SMS notifier that both implement one Notifier interface, then send through each.
examples.output:
[email] From shop@example.com to Ada: Your order has shipped
[sms] To Ada: Your order has sh...
examples.explanation: Both classes say `implements Notifier`, so `tsc` checks each one against the interface: a `channel` string, and a `send` that takes two strings and returns a string. A `readonly` field keeps its literal type, as the bubble shows, and `"email"` fits the interface's `string`. `EmailNotifier` also has a `from` field and a constructor, since an interface sets the least a class must have, not the most. The array is typed `Notifier[]`, so the loop may only use `channel` and `send`, and each object runs its own `send`: the email keeps the whole message, and the SMS cuts it to 20 characters.

examples.title: A missing method
examples.prompt: Declare that a class implements Notifier, but give its method another name.
examples.output:
main.ts(5,7): error TS2420: Class 'SmsNotifier' incorrectly implements interface 'Notifier'.
  Property 'send' is missing in type 'SmsNotifier' but required in type 'Notifier'.

examples.title: Shape is what counts
examples.prompt: Pass a class instance and a plain object to a function that asks for a Notifier.
examples.output:
Email to Ada: Your trial ends tomorrow
[dev] Ben <- Your trial ends tomorrow
[dev] Caro <- Your trial ends tomorrow

practice.title: Exporters
practice.prompt:
Write two exporters that turn the same stock rows into a CSV file and a JSON file.

1. Finish `CsvExporter`: its `export` returns the header line `sku,name,qty`, then one line per row with the same three fields, like `MUG-01,Mug,3`, all joined with `\n`.
2. Make `JsonExporter` implement `Exporter`, with the extension `json` and an `export` that returns `JSON.stringify(rows)`.
3. Add a `JsonExporter` to the `exporters` list.
4. Keep `export`: hidden type tests import `CsvExporter`, `JsonExporter`, and `Exporter` from your file, and Check also exports other rows.

Expected output:

```text
--- stock.csv
sku,name,qty
MUG-01,Mug,3
TEA-02,Green tea,12
--- stock.json
[{"sku":"MUG-01","name":"Mug","qty":3},{"sku":"TEA-02","name":"Green tea","qty":12}]
```

tests.output:
--- stock.csv
sku,name,qty
MUG-01,Mug,3
TEA-02,Green tea,12
--- stock.json
[{"sku":"MUG-01","name":"Mug","qty":3},{"sku":"TEA-02","name":"Green tea","qty":12}]

--- stock.csv
sku,name,qty
MUG-01,Mug,3
TEA-02,Green tea,12
--- stock.json
[{"sku":"MUG-01","name":"Mug","qty":3},{"sku":"TEA-02","name":"Green tea","qty":12}]
sku,name,qty
PEN-07,Pen,40
[{"sku":"PEN-07","name":"Pen","qty":40}]
sku,name,qty

typeTests.imports: import { CsvExporter, JsonExporter, type Exporter } from "./main.ts";

cases.name: an object without export isn't an Exporter
the extension is read-only
cases.code: const e: Exporter = new CsvExporter(); e.extension = "txt";

cases.name: any object of the right shape fits
cases.code: const e: Exporter = { extension: "txt", export: (rows) => String(rows.length) };

hints: Follow the notifiers example: each class says `implements Exporter` and declares every member the interface lists, with the same types.
For the CSV, map each row to one line, then put the header first: `["sku,name,qty", ...lines].join("\n")`.
`JsonExporter` needs `readonly extension = "json";` and `export(rows: readonly Row[]): string`, which returns `JSON.stringify(rows)`.

steps.title: Abstract classes

examples.title: A template method
examples.prompt: Write a Report base class that lays out every report the same way, and two reports that only supply their rows.
examples.output:
# Low stock
- MUG: 2 left
- PEN: 0 left
(2 rows)
# Signups
- Mon: 12
- Tue: 9
- Wed: 15
(3 rows)
examples.explanation: `render()` is written once, in the base class, and it fixes the layout: a title line, one bullet per row, and a count. Each subclass writes only what differs, its `rows()`. That's the template method pattern: the base class runs the steps, and subclasses fill in the step that varies. `reports` is typed `Report[]` even though a plain `Report` can never exist, and `render()` on each item runs the shared code with that report's own rows. Neither subclass marks `rows()` with `override`, because each one fills in an abstract member rather than replacing code.

examples.title: Abstract classes can't be created
examples.prompt: Extend an abstract class without writing its abstract method, and try to create the abstract class itself.
examples.output:
main.ts(9,7): error TS2515: Non-abstract class 'DraftReport' does not implement inherited abstract member rows from class 'Report'.
main.ts(11,16): error TS2511: Cannot create an instance of an abstract class.

examples.title: Shared state and a protected helper
examples.prompt: Give form validators a base class that holds their errors and formats each one, and two subclasses that only write their checks.
examples.output:
name is required
email must contain @
email must be lowercase
examples.explanation: The base class holds what every validator shares: a `field`, an `errors` list, and a `fail()` helper that formats each message the same way. `fail()` is `protected`, so the subclasses call it, while code outside can't add errors: `validator.fail("is wrong")` in the loop would be TS2445. Neither subclass has a constructor, so `new EmailValidator("email")` runs the base one and sets `field`. Each subclass writes only its `check()`. `form[validator.field]` is `string | undefined` under this course's config, so `??` passes an empty string for a field the form doesn't have.

practice.title: Price rules
practice.prompt:
Finish an abstract `PriceRule` class, and a rule that charges a minimum.

1. Declare `abstract apply(cents: number): number` in `PriceRule`, next to `applies`.
2. Make `run(cents)` return `this.apply(cents)` when `this.applies(cents)` is true, and `cents` unchanged otherwise.
3. Finish `MinimumCharge`: it applies when `cents` is below `minimumCents`, and its `apply` returns `minimumCents`.
4. Keep `export`: hidden type tests import `PriceRule`, `BulkDiscount`, and `MinimumCharge` from your file, and Check also runs other rules.

Expected output:

```text
bulk 12000 -> 10800
bulk 8000 -> 8000
minimum 300 -> 500
minimum 900 -> 900
```

cases.name: a rule must write apply
cases.code: class Free extends PriceRule { applies(): boolean { return true; } }

cases.name: a rule with both methods compiles
cases.code: class Free extends PriceRule { applies(): boolean { return true; } apply(): number { return 0; } }

cases.name: apply must return a number
cases.code: class Bad extends PriceRule { applies(): boolean { return true; } apply(): string { return "0"; } }

hints: The template method example declares `abstract rows(): string[];` and calls `this.rows()` from `render()`. `apply` and `run` work the same way.
In `MinimumCharge`, `applies` returns `cents < this.minimumCents`. `apply` doesn't need `cents`, so `apply(): number` can simply return `this.minimumCents`.

steps.title: Programming to an interface

examples.title: A repository behind an interface
examples.prompt: Give an order service its repository through the constructor, typed as an interface, and pass it an in-memory one.
examples.output:
Revenue: 1749 cents
ord_2 is for Ben
ord_9 is for nobody
examples.explanation: `OrderService` never mentions `InMemoryOrderRepository`. Its field and its constructor parameter are typed with the interface, so it works with anything that can save, find, and list orders. Here that's a `Map` wrapped in a class, the kind of repository tests use. In production the same service would get a repository that runs SQL, and not one line of the service would change. The lines at the bottom are the only place that picks an implementation, and they pass it in through the constructor.

examples.title: Swapping the clock
examples.prompt: Issue invoices that read the time through a Clock, and pass fixed clocks so every run prints the same dates.
examples.explanation: `InvoiceService` reads the time only through its `Clock`, so whoever creates it decides what time it is. `fixedClock` returns a clock that always answers with the same instant. That makes this program print the same lines on every run, and it lets you try a date near the end of the year, where the due date moves into 2027, without waiting for December. `systemClock` is what production passes: `new InvoiceService(systemClock)` would stamp invoices with the real date. A service that called `new Date()` itself could only ever be tested on today's date.

examples.title: A fake that records
examples.prompt: Check what a checkout service emails by passing it a fake mailer that writes each message down.
examples.output:
3 emails
ada@example.com: Order ord_1 confirmed
ben@example.com: Order ord_2 confirmed
sales@example.com: Large order ord_2
examples.explanation: `CheckoutService` only knows the `Mailer` interface, so it can't tell that `FakeMailer` sends nothing and just writes each message down. After the service runs, `mailer.sent` shows exactly what it tried to send, which is what a test checks: the customer always gets a confirmation, and sales hears about orders of $100 or more. The program keeps its own reference to the fake, `mailer`, to read `sent` afterward. Inside the service the field is typed `Mailer`, which has no `sent` at all.

practice.title: Currency service
practice.prompt:
Write a price service that converts money with whatever rate provider it's given.

1. Make `FixedRateProvider` implement `RateProvider`: keep the rates table in a private field, and look each rate up by a key like `USD->EUR`.
2. Give `PriceService` a private `RateProvider` field, set from its constructor, and pass `rates` to it.
3. Make `convert(cents, from, to)` return `<amount> <from> = <converted> <to>`, where the converted cents are `cents * rate` rounded to a whole number, and both amounts are divided by 100 and shown to 2 decimal places.
4. When the provider has no rate, return `no rate for <from>-><to>` instead.
5. Keep `export`: hidden type tests import `FixedRateProvider`, `PriceService`, and `RateProvider` from your file, and Check also gives the service other providers.

Expected output:

```text
25.00 USD = 23.00 EUR
10.00 EUR = 8.60 GBP
no rate for GBP->JPY
```

tests.output:
25.00 USD = 23.00 EUR
10.00 EUR = 8.60 GBP
no rate for GBP->JPY

25.00 USD = 23.00 EUR
10.00 EUR = 8.60 GBP
no rate for GBP->JPY
1.50 USD = 1.50 USD
1.50 USD = 3.00 CAD
no rate for EUR->USD

typeTests.imports: import { FixedRateProvider, PriceService, type RateProvider } from "./main.ts";

cases.name: a provider needs a rate method
any object with a rate method fits
rate returns a number or undefined
convert returns a string
cases.code: const s: string = new PriceService(new FixedRateProvider({})).convert(100, "USD", "EUR");

hints: Follow the repository example: declare `#rates: RateProvider;` in `PriceService`, take a `RateProvider` in the constructor, and assign it.
In `FixedRateProvider`, build the key with a template string, then read `this.#rates[key]`. Under this course's config that's already `number | undefined`, exactly what `rate` returns.
In `convert`, return the `no rate for` line when `rate === undefined`. Otherwise format `(cents / 100).toFixed(2)` and `(Math.round(cents * rate) / 100).toFixed(2)`.

recap:
- `class X implements Y` checks that the class has every member of the interface, with compatible types (TS2420, TS2416). It adds no code, and Node erases it.
- Any object of the right shape fits an interface, class or not. Interfaces don't exist at runtime, so `instanceof` can't test for one.
- An abstract class shares fields and methods, and declares `abstract` members that each subclass must write. Creating one is TS2511, and a subclass that skips a member is TS2515.
- A template method lives in the base class and calls the abstract steps, so each subclass writes only what differs.
- Dependency injection: type a class's dependencies as interfaces, receive them in the constructor, and keep them in fields.
- Production passes the real implementations, while tests and examples pass in-memory repositories, fixed clocks, and fakes that record.
